title: proxy
text:
Caddy is a web server that is often run as a reverse proxy. It receives the requests for your domain from the internet, fetches and renews an HTTPS certificate for the domain by itself, and passes each request to your app. Its config file is called a Caddyfile. A Caddyfile can start with a global block in braces, for settings such as the ACME account email, and then has one block per site.
Caddyfile builds a file with one site. Give it the domain and the name and port of the app to forward to; in a Compose stack, the app’s name is its service name. Each method adds a setting and returns a new Caddyfile:

email sets the address for the ACME account that requests certificates.
acme_dns gets certificates with a DNS-01 challenge through a DNS provider’s API, for when port 80 cannot be reached from outside. The token is read from the environment variable named by token_env.
cloudflared serves the site over plain http://, for use behind a Cloudflare Tunnel, which handles HTTPS itself. It also tells Caddy to trust the private addresses the tunnel arrives from and to read the visitor’s address from the Cf-Connecting-Ip header, so logs and client_ip show the visitor instead of the tunnel.
crowdsec checks each visitor’s IP address with a CrowdSec agent at api_url and blocks known attackers. The agent’s URL and key go in a global crowdsec block, the site block gets the crowdsec handler, and the global order crowdsec first runs it before every other handler. The plugin registers no place in Caddy’s directive order.
rate_limit allows each IP address requests requests per window.
max_body caps the size of a request body.
encode turns on response compression, which Caddy leaves off by default. Name the encodings to choose them and their order, as in encode('zstd', 'gzip').
log turns on access logs. They go to stderr unless you pass output: a file path such as '/var/log/caddy/access.log', or a Caddy log writer such as 'stdout', 'discard' or 'net localhost:9999'. A file output rotates with roll_size (such as '50MiB'), roll_keep (files kept) and roll_keep_for (such as '2160h'); format sets the encoder, such as 'json'.
spa serves a single-page app’s static files from static_dir instead of forwarding to the app, and answers any path that is not a file with index.html.
upstreams forwards to several copies of the app, one per port in ports, such as one per worker process. The keywords become reverse_proxy options: lb_policy picks how requests are shared, lb_try_duration and lb_try_interval retry a failed request on another copy, and health_uri, health_interval, health_timeout and fail_duration take a copy out of rotation while it fails its health check. With handle=True the proxy sits inside a handle block, which you need when raw blocks use handle with a matcher: Caddy runs only the first handle that matches, so the proxy becomes the fallback.
raw adds a block of Caddyfile text as it is, for directives the builder has no method for. Indent its lines after the first with tabs as they should appear.
comment adds a # line to the site block, and notes adds comments at the ends of lines. notes takes a dict from the start of a line, such as 'encode', to its comment.

The file ends with a newline, and a blank line separates the global block from the site.
The DNS provider behind acme_dns, and the crowdsec and rate_limit settings, come from Caddy plugins that the official caddy:2 image does not include. The image you run must have them built in. caddy_svc below picks such an image for Cloudflare DNS and for CrowdSec.

text:
Caddyfile presets
Most sites need only a few of those settings. caddy builds a Caddyfile from keyword arguments, one per option, and returns it; nothing is written until you call .save(). dns is ignored when cloudflared=True, because behind a tunnel Caddy fetches no certificates at all. The token variable defaults to the provider’s name in capitals followed by _API_TOKEN, such as CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN.
caddy_api is caddy with settings suited to an API: a limit of 200 requests a minute from each IP address, a 50 MB cap on request bodies, and compression. The examples below print the file each combination writes.


source

caddy_api
def caddy_api(
    domain, app:str='app', port:int=5001, email:NoneType=None, dns:NoneType=None, dns_token_env:NoneType=None,
    cloudflared:bool=False, crowdsec:bool=False, crowdsec_url:str='http://crowdsec:8080', max_body:str='50m',
    rate:str='200', rate_window:str='1m'
)->str:
Build a caddy Caddyfile for an API, adding a per-IP rate limit, a cap on request bodies and compression.




source

caddy
def caddy(
    domain, # domain to serve, such as example.com or app.example.com
    app:str='app', # name of the app to forward to; in Compose, its service name
    port:int=5001, # port the app listens on
    email:NoneType=None, # ACME account email, so Let's Encrypt can write to you about certificates
    dns:NoneType=None, # DNS provider for a DNS-01 challenge, such as 'cloudflare' or 'duckdns', for when port 80 is not reachable
    dns_token_env:NoneType=None, # environment variable holding the DNS provider's API token; defaults to {DNS}_API_TOKEN, such as CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN
    crowdsec:bool=False, # check visitors against a CrowdSec agent; needs a Caddy image with the CrowdSec plugin and a separate crowdsec service
    crowdsec_url:str='http://crowdsec:8080', # URL of the CrowdSec agent; the default is a service called crowdsec on the same Compose network
    cloudflared:bool=False, # serve plain http:// behind a Cloudflare Tunnel; Caddy then fetches no certificates and dns is ignored
    encode:bool=False, # turn on response compression, which Caddy leaves off by default
    access_log:bool=False, # log every request to stderr; Caddy writes no access log by default
)->__main__.Caddyfile:
Build a Caddyfile that forwards domain to app:port, with optional ACME email, DNS-01 challenge, CrowdSec, tunnel mode, compression and access log.



cf = str(caddy('myapp.example.com', port=5001))
assert 'myapp.example.com {' in cf
assert 'reverse_proxy app:5001' in cf
assert cf.count('{') == 1
print(cf)

myapp.example.com {
    reverse_proxy app:5001
}



cf = str(caddy('myapp.example.com', port=5001, dns='cloudflare', email='me@example.com'))
assert 'email me@example.com' in cf
assert 'acme_dns cloudflare {$CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}' in cf
print(cf)

{
    email me@example.com
}
myapp.example.com {
    tls {
        acme_dns cloudflare {$CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}
    }
    reverse_proxy app:5001
}



cf = str(caddy('myapp.example.com', port=5001, crowdsec=True))
assert 'api_url http://crowdsec:8080' in cf
assert 'crowdsec' in cf
assert 'api_key {$CROWDSEC_API_KEY}' in cf

assert g == '{\n\torder crowdsec first\n\tcrowdsec {\n\t\tapi_url http://crowdsec:8080\n\t\tapi_key {$CROWDSEC_API_KEY}\n\t}\n}', g
assert '\tcrowdsec\n' in site and 'api_url' not in site
assert str(caddy('a.com', email='a@b.c', crowdsec=True)).startswith('{\n\temail a@b.c\n\torder crowdsec first\n')
print(cf)

myapp.example.com {
    crowdsec {
        api_url http://crowdsec:8080
        api_key {$CROWDSEC_API_KEY}
    }
    reverse_proxy app:5001
}

assert 'reverse_proxy app:5001' in cf
print(cf)

http://myapp.example.com {
    reverse_proxy app:5001
}

assert 'rate_limit' in cf and 'max_size 50m' in cf and 'encode' in cf
assert 'reverse_proxy app:5001' in cf

cf = str(caddy_api('myapp.example.com', crowdsec=True, max_body='100m', rate='50', rate_window='30s'))
assert 'crowdsec' in cf and 'events 50' in cf and 'window 30s' in cf and 'max_size 100m' in cf
print('caddy_api() with crowdsec OK')

cf = str(Caddyfile('myapp.example.com').spa())
assert 'try_files {path} /index.html' in cf and 'file_server' in cf
assert 'reverse_proxy' not in cf
print('spa() OK')

cf = str(caddy('myapp.example.com', encode=True, access_log=True))
assert '\tencode' in cf and '\tlog' in cf
print('encode() and log() OK')

cf = str(Caddyfile('myapp.example.com').log(output='/var/log/caddy/access.log'))
assert '\t\toutput file /var/log/caddy/access.log\n' in cf
for o in ('stdout', 'discard', 'file /tmp/a.log', 'net localhost:9999'): assert f'\t\toutput {o}\n' in str(Caddyfile('a.com').log(o))
assert str(Caddyfile('a.com').log()).splitlines()[1] == '\tlog'
cf = str(Caddyfile('a.com').log('/data/logs/access.log', roll_size='50MiB', roll_keep=20, roll_keep_for='2160h', format='json'))
assert '\tlog {\n\t\toutput file /data/logs/access.log {\n\t\t\troll_size 50MiB\n\t\t\troll_keep 20\n\t\t\troll_keep_for 2160h\n\t\t}\n\t\tformat json\n\t}' in cf
for k,v in dict(roll_size='50MiB', roll_keep=20, roll_keep_for='2160h').items():
    cf = str(Caddyfile('a.com').log('/l.log', **{k: v}))
    assert f'\t\toutput file /l.log {{\n\t\t\t{k} {v}\n\t\t}}\n\t}}' in cf
assert '\tlog {\n\t\tformat json\n\t}' in str(Caddyfile('a.com').log(format='json'))
test_fail(lambda: Caddyfile('a.com').log('stdout', roll_keep=5), contains='file output')
print('log(output=...) OK')

caddy_api() OK
caddy_api() with crowdsec OK
spa() OK
encode() and log() OK
log(output=...) OK



cf = (Caddyfile('ex.com', port=5001).cloudflared().comment('three workers').log('/data/access.log', roll_keep=5, format='json')
      .encode('zstd', 'gzip').raw('@hashed path /js/*\n\thandle @hashed {\n\t\tfile_server\n\t}')
      .upstreams(range(5001, 5003), handle=True, lb_policy='round_robin', health_uri='/health')
      .notes({'trusted_proxies': 'the tunnel', 'client_ip_headers': 'the reader', 'encode': 'smaller pages', 'roll_keep': 'five files'}))
test_eq(str(cf), """{
    servers {
        trusted_proxies static private_ranges   # the tunnel
        client_ip_headers Cf-Connecting-Ip      # the reader
    }
}

http://ex.com {
    # three workers
    log {
        output file /data/access.log {
            roll_keep 5   # five files
        }
        format json
    }
    encode zstd gzip   # smaller pages
    @hashed path /js/*
    handle @hashed {
        file_server
    }
    handle {
        reverse_proxy app:5001 app:5002 {
            lb_policy round_robin
            health_uri /health
        }
    }
}
""")
test_eq(str(Caddyfile('a.com').upstreams([5001, 5002])), 'a.com {\n\treverse_proxy app:5001 app:5002\n}\n')
test_eq(str(Caddyfile('a.com').encode()), 'a.com {\n\tencode\n\treverse_proxy app:5001\n}\n')
print('upstreams, raw, comment and notes OK')

text:
Services
These functions return the settings for one Compose service, as a dict to pass to Compose.svc with **. Every service joins a network called web and restarts unless you stop it, so declare .network('web') in the stack.
caddy_svc writes the Caddyfile from caddy to conf and returns the Caddy service. The service mounts that Caddyfile, keeps certificates and state in the caddy_data and caddy_config volumes, starts after the app service, and publishes ports 80 and 443 unless cloudflared=True. It also picks an image that has the plugins your options need:







options
image




none, or only cloudflared=True
caddy:2


crowdsec=True
serfriz/caddy-crowdsec:latest


dns='cloudflare'
serfriz/caddy-cloudflare:latest


dns='cloudflare' and crowdsec=True
ghcr.io/buildplan/csdp-caddy:latest



For any other DNS provider, pass an image with that provider’s plugin as image, as the duckdns test below does. The service passes the DNS token and CROWDSEC_API_KEY through from the host’s environment. An absolute conf is mounted from that path. A relative one is mounted as ./ plus its file name, so in that case save the Compose file in the same folder as the Caddyfile. mount sets the mounted path yourself, such as ./Caddyfile for an absolute conf beside the Compose file. Pass your own Caddyfile as caddyfile to write it instead of the one built from the options, or save=False to write nothing.


source

caddy_svc
def caddy_svc(
    domain, app:str='app', port:int=5001, *, dns:NoneType=None, email:NoneType=None, crowdsec:bool=False,
    cloudflared:bool=False, conf:str='Caddyfile', caddyfile:NoneType=None, save:bool=True, mount:NoneType=None, **kw
):
Write the Caddyfile to conf and return a Caddy service for Compose.svc, with an image that has the plugins the options need.



import os, time, tempfile, subprocess
from fastcore.all import urlread, Path


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile')
    assert kw['image'] == 'caddy:2'
    assert kw['ports'] == ['80:80', '443:443', '443:443/udp']
    assert kw['depends_on'] == ['app']
    print('caddy_svc() basic OK')

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', cloudflared=True, conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile')
    assert 'ports' not in kw
    assert kw['image'] == 'caddy:2'
    assert '\nhttp://ex.com {' in Path(f'{tmp}/Caddyfile').read_text()
    print('caddy_svc() cloudflared OK')

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', crowdsec=True, conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile')
    assert kw['image'] == 'serfriz/caddy-crowdsec:latest'
    assert 'CROWDSEC_API_KEY=${CROWDSEC_API_KEY}' in kw['environment']
    print('caddy_svc() crowdsec OK')

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', crowdsec=True, cloudflared=True, conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile')
    assert kw['image'] == 'serfriz/caddy-crowdsec:latest'
    assert 'ports' not in kw
    print('caddy_svc() crowdsec+cloudflared OK')

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', dns='cloudflare', conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile')
    assert kw['image'] == 'serfriz/caddy-cloudflare:latest'
    assert 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}' in kw['environment']
    print('caddy_svc() cloudflare-dns OK')

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', dns='cloudflare', crowdsec=True, conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile')
    assert kw['image'] == 'ghcr.io/buildplan/csdp-caddy:latest'
    assert 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}' in kw['environment']
    assert 'CROWDSEC_API_KEY=${CROWDSEC_API_KEY}' in kw['environment']
    print('caddy_svc() cloudflare-dns+crowdsec OK')

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.duckdns.org', dns='duckdns', conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile', image='serfriz/caddy-duckdns:latest')
    assert kw['image'] == 'serfriz/caddy-duckdns:latest'
    assert 'DUCKDNS_API_TOKEN=${DUCKDNS_API_TOKEN}' in kw['environment']
    cf = Path(f'{tmp}/Caddyfile').read_text()
    assert 'acme_dns duckdns {$DUCKDNS_API_TOKEN}' in cf
    print('caddy_svc() duckdns OK')

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile', caddyfile=Caddyfile('ex.com').encode(), mount='./Caddyfile')
    assert './Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile' in kw['volumes']
    test_eq(Path(f'{tmp}/Caddyfile').read_text(), 'ex.com {\n\tencode\n\treverse_proxy app:5001\n}\n')
    caddy_svc('ex.com', conf=f'{tmp}/Other', save=False)
    assert not Path(f'{tmp}/Other').exists()
    print('caddy_svc() caddyfile, save and mount OK')

kw = caddy_svc('ex.com', conf='config/Caddyfile', save=False)
assert './config/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile' in kw['volumes']

caddy_svc() basic OK
caddy_svc() cloudflared OK
caddy_svc() crowdsec OK
caddy_svc() crowdsec+cloudflared OK
caddy_svc() cloudflare-dns OK
caddy_svc() cloudflare-dns+crowdsec OK
caddy_svc() duckdns OK


cloudflared_svc returns the Cloudflare Tunnel service. The cloudflared container connects out to Cloudflare and carries your site’s traffic back over that connection, so the server needs no open inbound port. token_env is the value given to the container’s TUNNEL_TOKEN; the default, ${CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN}, makes Compose read the token from the host’s CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN variable. Where the tunnel sends traffic is normally set in the Cloudflare dashboard, and url passes it on the command line instead, for example url='http://caddy'.


source

cloudflared_svc
def cloudflared_svc(
    token_env:str='${CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN}', url:NoneType=None, **kw
):
Return a Cloudflare Tunnel service for Compose.svc; url sets where the tunnel sends traffic, such as http://caddy.



kw = cloudflared_svc()
assert kw['image'] == 'cloudflare/cloudflared:latest'
assert kw['command'] == 'tunnel --no-autoupdate run'
assert 'TUNNEL_TOKEN=${CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN}' in kw['environment']
print('cloudflared_svc() OK')

kw2 = cloudflared_svc(url='http://caddy')
assert kw2['command'] == 'tunnel --no-autoupdate run --url http://caddy'
print('cloudflared_svc() with url OK')

cloudflared_svc() OK
cloudflared_svc() with url OK


CrowdSec keeps a shared list of IP addresses known for attacks, and Caddy’s CrowdSec plugin asks a local CrowdSec agent about each visitor. crowdsec returns the agent service. collections are the CrowdSec rule sets it installs; the default covers Linux, Caddy and known HTTP exploits. The agent registers a bouncer, CrowdSec’s name for a client that enforces its decisions, called caddy, with the key from the host’s CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY variable. caddy_svc(crowdsec=True) gives Caddy its key from CROWDSEC_API_KEY, so set both variables to the same value. The agent keeps its data and config in the crowdsec-db and crowdsec-config volumes, which the stack must declare.


source

crowdsec
def crowdsec(
    collections:NoneType=None, bouncer_key_env:str='CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY', **kw
):
Return a CrowdSec agent service for Compose.svc, with the bouncer key for Caddy read from bouncer_key_env.



kw = crowdsec()
assert kw['image'] == 'crowdsecurity/crowdsec:latest'
assert any('crowdsecurity/caddy' in e for e in kw['environment'])
assert 'BOUNCER_KEY_caddy=${CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY}' in kw['environment']
assert any('crowdsec-db' in v for v in kw['volumes'])
print('crowdsec() OK')

kw2 = crowdsec(collections=['crowdsecurity/linux', 'crowdsecurity/nginx'])
assert any('crowdsecurity/nginx' in e for e in kw2['environment'])
print('crowdsec() custom collections OK')

crowdsec() OK
crowdsec() custom collections OK

text:
Example stacks
Five complete stacks for an app behind Caddy, from the simplest to the most locked down. Each one prints its Compose file. To run one, save it with dc.save('docker-compose.yml') and run docker compose up -d.

Stack A: Caddy fetches certificates itself, and ports 80 and 443 are open.
Stack B: a Cloudflare Tunnel carries the traffic, and no port is open.
Stack C: stack B with CrowdSec checking visitors.
Stack D: Caddy gets its certificate with a DNS-01 challenge through Cloudflare, with the ports open and no tunnel.
Stack E: stack D with CrowdSec.


tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()

dc = (Compose()
    .svc('app', build='.', networks=['web'], restart='unless-stopped')
    .svc('caddy', **caddy_svc('myapp.example.com', port=5001, conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile'))
    .network('web', driver='bridge').volume('caddy_data').volume('caddy_config'))

d = dc.to_dict()
assert d['services']['caddy']['image'] == 'caddy:2'
assert '80:80' in d['services']['caddy']['ports']
print('=== Stack A: Direct (Caddy auto-TLS) ===')
print(dc)

=== Stack A: Direct (Caddy auto-TLS) ===
services:
  app:
    build: .
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    depends_on:
    - app
    ports:
    - 80:80
    - 443:443
    - 443:443/udp
    volumes:
    - /private/var/folders/kg/9vdw4mdd1fs58svgh4k1qhr09x7dqh/T/tmp2pn1i7ra/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
    - caddy_data:/data
    - caddy_config:/config
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
networks:
  web:
    driver: bridge
volumes:
  caddy_data: null
  caddy_config: null




tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
dc = (Compose()
    .svc('app', build='.', networks=['web'], restart='unless-stopped')
    .svc('caddy', **caddy_svc('myapp.example.com', port=5001, cloudflared=True, conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile'))
    .svc('cloudflared', **cloudflared_svc())
    .network('web').volume('caddy_data').volume('caddy_config'))

d = dc.to_dict()
assert 'ports' not in d['services']['caddy']
assert d['services']['cloudflared']['image'] == 'cloudflare/cloudflared:latest'
print('=== Stack B: Cloudflared (zero open ports) ===')
print(dc)

=== Stack B: Cloudflared (zero open ports) ===
services:
  app:
    build: .
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    depends_on:

Integration test: FastHTML, Caddy and cloudflared
This test starts a real stack and checks that the app can be reached over the internet. It is skipped in the docs build and by nbdev_test. To run it you need:

a Cloudflare Tunnel, created in the Cloudflare Zero Trust dashboard under Tunnels, with its token in the CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN environment variable;
a public hostname on that tunnel that sends traffic to http://caddy;
DOMAIN, set at the top of the cell, changed to that hostname.

title: dockeasy
text:
dockeasy writes the files that run an app in Docker containers, and runs Docker from Python.
A Dockerfile is the recipe Docker follows to build an image: a base image to start from, files to copy in, commands to run, and the command to start. A container is a running copy of an image. A Compose file, docker-compose.yml, describes several containers that run together, such as a web app, its database and a proxy. Each named application component is a service. Compose creates the containers of each service. Writing these files by hand needs exact syntax and quoting. With dockeasy you build each file with Python method calls, print it to check it, and save it.
Dockerfile and Compose write the two files. Builders such as python_app and go_app return a ready-made Dockerfile for a common kind of project. detect_app checks your project’s files and returns a Dockerfile from the matching builder. The proxy helpers write a Caddyfile, the config for the Caddy web server. Caddy takes requests from the internet, handles HTTPS certificates and passes the requests on to your app. Thin wrappers around the docker command build images and run containers. A small store keeps config values and secrets.

title: dockeasy
text:
Install
pip install dockeasy
Everything is exported from the top-level package:

from dockeasy import *

title: dockeasy
text:
Dockerfiles in Python
Start with an empty Dockerfile() and call one method per instruction. from_ sets the base image, with a trailing underscore because from is a Python keyword. copy copies files from your project into the image, run runs a shell command while the image is built, expose records the port the app listens on, and cmd sets the command the container runs when it starts. Printing the object shows the file it will write.
Each method returns a new Dockerfile and leaves the one you called it on unchanged, so you can keep a base recipe in a variable and extend it in different ways.

df = (Dockerfile()
    .from_('python:3.12-slim')
    .workdir('/app')
    .copy('requirements.txt', '.')
    .run('pip install -r requirements.txt')
    .copy('.', '.')
    .expose(8000)
    .cmd(['python', 'main.py']))

print(df)

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "main.py"]



Multi-stage builds
A multi-stage build compiles your app in one image and runs it in a second, smaller one, so compilers and source code stay out of the image you ship. Each from_ call starts a new stage. Name a stage with as_=, then copy files out of it with copy(..., from_='builder'). Here a Go program is built in the golang image and only the compiled binary is copied into a minimal distroless image:

df = (Dockerfile()
    .from_('golang:1.22-alpine', as_='builder')
    .workdir('/src')
    .copy('.', '.')
    .run('go build -o /app .')
    .from_('gcr.io/distroless/static')
    .copy('/app', '/app', from_='builder')
    .cmd(['/app']))

print(df)

FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /app .
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
COPY --from=builder /app /app
CMD ["/app"]




Build cache mounts
Docker reruns a RUN step whenever the files copied in before it change, and a package install then downloads everything again. run_mount writes RUN --mount=type=cache,..., which keeps a folder, such as pip’s or uv’s download cache, from one build to the next. Pass the cache folder as target:

df = (Dockerfile()
    .from_('python:3.12-slim')
    .workdir('/app')
    .copy('requirements.txt', '.')
    .run_mount('pip install -r requirements.txt', target='/root/.cache/pip')
    .copy('.', '.')
    .cmd(['python', 'main.py']))

print(df)

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "main.py"]

title: dockeasy
text:
Ready-made Dockerfiles
For common kinds of project you do not need to write the Dockerfile yourself. Each function below returns a complete Dockerfile, which you can print, extend with more method calls, or save.

Python with uv
python_app is for a Python project managed with uv, with a pyproject.toml and a uv.lock. By default it writes a two-stage build. The first stage runs in uv’s own image and installs your locked dependencies into a .venv folder. The second stage starts from python:3.13-slim and copies the app folder across, .venv included, so uv itself stays behind. The container runs python main.py on port 8000; cmd and port change them.

python_app()

FROM ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.13-bookworm AS builder
WORKDIR /app
ENV UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1
ENV UV_LINK_MODE=copy
COPY pyproject.toml .
COPY uv.lock .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv uv sync --frozen --no-dev
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app /app
ENV PATH=/app/.venv/bin:$PATH
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "main.py"]


pkgs installs system packages with apt-get, vols creates the folders you plan to mount volumes on, and healthcheck adds a HEALTHCHECK that requests that path on the app’s port every 30 seconds. The slim Python image has no curl, so the check uses Python’s urllib unless pkgs installs curl, as it does here. multistage=False gives a single-stage build that installs uv with pip, and adding req=True to that installs from requirements.txt instead of pyproject.toml.

python_app(pkgs=['libpq-dev', 'curl'], vols=['/app/data'], healthcheck='/health')

FROM ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.13-bookworm AS builder
WORKDIR /app
ENV UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1
ENV UV_LINK_MODE=copy
COPY pyproject.toml .
COPY uv.lock .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv uv sync --frozen --no-dev
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y libpq-dev curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY --from=builder /app /app
ENV PATH=/app/.venv/bin:$PATH
RUN mkdir -p /app/data
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "main.py"]




FastHTML app
fasthtml_app is python_app with the settings a FastHTML app usually needs: port 5001, the command python app.py, and a single-stage build. You can still override any of them.

fasthtml_app()

FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install uv
COPY pyproject.toml .
RUN uv sync --no-dev
ENV PATH=/app/.venv/bin:$PATH
COPY . .
EXPOSE 5001
CMD ["python", "app.py"]




Go app
go_app downloads the modules and compiles a static binary in golang:1.22-alpine, then copies only the binary into gcr.io/distroless/static, a minimal image with no shell or package manager. The app listens on port 8080, and binary names the output file.

go_app()

FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder

text:
Docker Compose
Compose writes a docker-compose.yml in the same way that Dockerfile writes a Dockerfile. svc adds a service. Give it either image, a published image to run, or build, the folder holding the Dockerfile to build. ports maps host ports to container ports, env sets environment variables, volumes attaches named volumes or host folders at paths inside the container, and depends_on names services that must start first. Any other keyword, such as networks or restart, is copied into the service unchanged. network and volume declare the networks and named volumes that the services use.
The api service below passes a Dockerfile object as build, which svc writes as build: ., meaning the current folder. python_app().save() writes that Dockerfile into the current folder and the final .save() writes docker-compose.yml there too. Running this cell leaves both files next to the notebook.

dc = (Compose()
    .svc('web',  image='nginx', ports={80: 80}, networks=['backend'])
    .svc('api',  build=python_app().save(), ports={8000: 8000},
         env={'DATABASE_URL': 'postgresql://db/app'},
         depends_on=['db'], networks=['backend'])
    .svc('db',   image='postgres:16',
         env={'POSTGRES_PASSWORD': 'secret'},
         volumes={'pgdata': '/var/lib/postgresql/data'})
    .network('backend')
    .volume('pgdata')).save()
dc

services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    ports:
    - 80:80
    networks:
    - backend
  api:
    depends_on:
    - db
    ports:
    - 8000:8000
    build: .
    environment:
    - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://db/app
    networks:
    - backend
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
    - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret
    volumes:
    - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
networks:
  backend: null
volumes:
  pgdata: null


save writes the file, to docker-compose.yml by default. up saves it and runs docker compose up -d, and down runs docker compose down. Their keyword arguments become command-line flags. v=True adds -v, which also deletes the stack’s named volumes. The docs build does not run the cell below. The stack above is an illustration, and the cell fails if you run it as it is.

dc.save('docker-compose.yml')
dc.up()
dc.down(v=True)

text:
Building and running containers
These functions wrap the docker command so that a script or notebook can build an image, run it and clean up without leaving Python. They need Docker installed and running, so these cells are not run when the docs are built, and the outputs shown come from an earlier run.
Dockerfile.build saves the Dockerfile into the folder path and builds it with docker compose build, which uses the Docker daemon’s own BuildKit. The separate buildx plugin is not needed. It returns the tag. no_creds=True builds with a copy of your Docker config that has the credential helpers removed. drun runs a container and returns what it printed, and rmi removes an image. The example below saves its Dockerfile into an empty temporary folder. For your own application, pass the folder of that application as path:

tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
df = (Dockerfile()
    .from_('alpine')
    .cmd(['echo', 'hello from docker']))

tag = df.build(tag='myapp:latest', path=tmp, no_creds=True)
print(f'Built: {tag}')

out = drun(tag, remove=True)
print(out.strip())

rmi(tag, force=True)
print('Cleaned up.')

Built: myapp:latest
hello from docker
Cleaned up.


With detach=True, drun starts the container in the background and returns its ID. ports maps container ports to host ports, the other way round from Compose: {'80/tcp': 8080} makes the container’s port 80 reachable on port 8080 of your machine. With check=True, the default, drun watches the container for up to two seconds and raises RuntimeError, with the container’s logs, if it stops in that time. containers lists the names of running containers, logs returns the last n lines of a container’s log, and stop and rm stop and remove it:

cid = drun('nginx', detach=True, ports={'80/tcp': 8080}, name='my-nginx', check=True)

print(containers())
print(logs('my-nginx', n=5))

stop('my-nginx')
rm('my-nginx')

Smoke-test an image
test runs a command in a throwaway container from an image and returns True if the command exits with status 0, and False otherwise. It is a quick check, in CI for example, that an image starts and has what your app needs:

assert test('python:3.12-slim', ['python', '-c', 'import sys; sys.exit(0)'])
assert not test('python:3.12-slim', ['python', '-c', 'raise SystemExit(1)'])

text:
Config and secrets
Deploy scripts need settings such as a server’s IP address, and secrets such as API tokens, and these should not be written into the code. env_set saves a value in ~/.config/fastops/.env, a file only you can read, and also sets it in os.environ so the running process sees it straight away. env_get reads os.environ first and falls back to the file:

env_set('VPS_IP',    '1.2.3.4')
env_set('APP_NAME',  'my-app')

print(env_get('VPS_IP'))
print(env_get('APP_NAME'))

1.2.3.4
my-app


secret_set is for sensitive values. It stores the value in the system keychain through the keyring package, such as the macOS Keychain, and raises RuntimeError on a machine with no keychain, as on most servers. Pass save=True to also write the value, in plain text, to the same .env file and to os.environ. With save=True and no keychain, secret_set warns that the .env file holds the only copy and writes it. secret_get looks in the keychain first, then os.environ, then the file, and returns default if none of them has the key.

secret_set('FOO', 'bar', save=True)
print(secret_get('FOO'))

bar


secrets reads several keys at once and returns a dict of the ones that have a value. Missing keys are left out without a warning.

secret_set('DATABASE_URL', 'postgresql://...', save=True)
cfg = secrets('FOO', 'DATABASE_URL', 'MISSING_KEY')
cfg

{'FOO': 'bar', 'DATABASE_URL': 'postgresql://...'}

text:
Reverse proxy
A reverse proxy sits in front of your app and receives the requests that arrive from the internet. Caddy is a web server that does this job and also fetches and renews HTTPS certificates for your domain from Let’s Encrypt on its own, using the ACME protocol. You configure it with a file called a Caddyfile.
caddy returns a Caddyfile object for a domain. Unless you say otherwise, it forwards requests to the service called app on port 5001. Print it to see the file, or call .save() to write it. The simplest one is a single site block with a reverse_proxy line:

print(caddy('myapp.example.com'))

myapp.example.com {
    reverse_proxy app:5001
}


To issue a certificate, Let’s Encrypt normally connects to your server on port 80 to check that you control the domain. When that port is closed, Caddy can prove control with a DNS-01 challenge instead, by creating a DNS record through your DNS provider’s API. Pass the provider as dns. Caddy reads the API token from an environment variable, CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN here, and dns_token_env names a different one. email is the address Let’s Encrypt can write to about your certificates. The official Caddy image has no DNS provider plugins. caddy_svc below switches to an image that has the Cloudflare plugin.

print(caddy('myapp.example.com', dns='cloudflare', email='me@example.com'))

{
    email me@example.com
}
myapp.example.com {
    tls {
        acme_dns cloudflare {$CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}
    }
    reverse_proxy app:5001
}



Running Caddy behind a Cloudflare Tunnel
A Cloudflare Tunnel lets visitors reach your server without opening any inbound port. A program called cloudflared runs in a container next to your app, makes an outgoing connection to Cloudflare, and receives your site’s traffic over it. Cloudflare serves HTTPS to the visitor, so Caddy only needs to speak plain HTTP.
caddy_svc writes the Caddyfile to conf and returns the settings for a Caddy service, ready to pass to Compose.svc with **. With cloudflared=True the Caddyfile serves plain http:// and the service publishes no ports. cloudflared_svc returns the settings for the tunnel container, which reads its token from the CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN environment variable on the host. Both services join a network called web, and Caddy keeps its certificates and state in the caddy_data and caddy_config volumes, so the Compose file declares all three. To add CrowdSec, which blocks IP addresses known for attacks, see caddy_svc(crowdsec=True) and crowdsec on the proxy page.

import tempfile
tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()

dc = (Compose()
    .svc('app', build='.', networks=['web'], restart='unless-stopped')
    .svc('caddy', **caddy_svc('myapp.example.com', cloudflared=True, conf=f'{tmp}/Caddyfile'))
    .svc('cloudflared', **cloudflared_svc())
    .network('web').volume('caddy_data').volume('caddy_config'))

print(dc)

services:
  app:
    build: .
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    depends_on:
    - app
    volumes:
    - /private/var/folders/kg/9vdw4mdd1fs58svgh4k1qhr09x7dqh/T/tmpv94f2dqp/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
    - caddy_data:/data
    - caddy_config:/config
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run
    environment:
    - TUNNEL_TOKEN=${CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN}
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
networks:
  web: null
volumes:
  caddy_data: null
  caddy_config: null

Several functions on this page take keyword arguments and pass them on to a command-line tool, and mk_flags does the conversion. A one-letter keyword becomes a short flag, so d=True gives -d and f='x' gives -f x. A longer one becomes a long flag with underscores turned into hyphens, so remove_orphans=True gives --remove-orphans and name='web' gives --name=web. Keywords set to False or None are left out, and positional arguments come first. With short=False, every keyword becomes a long flag.

def mk_flags(
    *a, short:bool=True, sym:str='=', **kw
):
Turn keyword arguments into command-line flags: one-letter keys become -k [value] and longer keys --key[=value].




A Dockerfile is a list of instructions, one per line, each starting with a keyword such as FROM, RUN or COPY. The private helpers below (_from, _run, _copy and so on) each format one instruction. They take care of the details that are easy to get wrong by hand: joining an image and its tag, writing a command list in the JSON form Docker expects, and chaining several shell commands into a single RUN with &&. You do not call them directly; the Dockerfile methods do.
The tests after the helpers show the exact line each one writes.

assert _instr('RUN', 'echo hello') == 'RUN echo hello'
assert _from('python', '3.11') == 'FROM python:3.11'
assert _from('ubuntu', as_='builder') == 'FROM ubuntu AS builder'
assert _from('alpine') == 'FROM alpine'
assert _run('apt-get update') == 'RUN apt-get update'
r = _run(['apt-get update', 'apt-get install -y curl'])
assert 'apt-get update && ' in r
assert 'apt-get install -y curl' in r
assert _apt_install('curl', 'wget', y=True) == 'RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl wget && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*'
assert _apt_install('git', clean=False) == 'RUN apt-get update && apt-get install git'
assert _cmd(['python', 'app.py']) == 'CMD ["python", "app.py"]'
assert _cmd('echo hello') == 'CMD echo hello'
assert _copy('.', '/app') == 'COPY . /app'
assert _copy('/build/out', '/app', from_='builder') == 'COPY --from=builder /build/out /app'
assert _copy('app/', '.', link=True) == 'COPY --link app/ .'
assert _copy('/app', '/app', from_='builder', link=True) == 'COPY --from=builder --link /app /app'
assert _workdir('/app') == 'WORKDIR /app'
assert _env('PATH', '/usr/local/bin') == 'ENV PATH=/usr/local/bin'
assert _env('DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive') == 'ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive'
assert _expose(8080) == 'EXPOSE 8080'
assert _entrypoint(['python', '-m', 'flask']) == 'ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-m", "flask"]'
assert _arg('VERSION', '1.0') == 'ARG VERSION=1.0'
assert _arg('VERSION') == 'ARG VERSION'
assert _label(version='1.0', maintainer='me') == 'LABEL version="1.0" maintainer="me"'
assert _volume('/data') == 'VOLUME /data'
assert _volume(['/data', '/logs']) == 'VOLUME ["/data", "/logs"]'
assert _shell(['/bin/bash', '-c']) == 'SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]'
assert 'CMD curl' in _healthcheck('curl -f http://localhost/', i='30s')
assert _healthcheck('curl localhost', i='30s', t='10s') == 'HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s CMD curl localhost'
assert _healthcheck('curl localhost') == 'HEALTHCHECK CMD curl localhost'
assert _on_build(_run('echo triggered')) == 'ONBUILD RUN echo triggered'




Dockerfile holds the instruction lines in order. It has one method per Dockerfile keyword, named in lower case, and each method returns a new Dockerfile with the line added, so calls chain. print shows the file, and save writes it, to ./Dockerfile by default. A keyword without its own method still works: df.maintainer('me') adds MAINTAINER me, and df('healthcheck', 'NONE') does the same by name.
run_mount adds a RUN line with a --mount option. The default is a cache mount, a folder such as pip’s download cache that Docker keeps between builds; give its path as target.
_parse, below, reads Dockerfile text into a list of lines. It joins lines continued with a backslash and drops blank lines and comments, and Dockerfile.load uses it.

parsed = _parse("# comment\nFROM python:3.11\nRUN apt-get update && \\\n    apt-get install -y curl\nCOPY . /app")
print(parsed)
assert len(parsed) == 3
assert parsed[0] == 'FROM python:3.11'
assert 'apt-get install -y curl' in parsed[1]

['FROM python:3.11', 'RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl', 'COPY . /app']

These functions wrap the Docker command-line tool for the usual loop: build an image from a Dockerfile, run a container from it, and check that a command succeeds inside it. They need Docker installed and its daemon running.
Cli is a small base class for wrapping a command-line tool, and Docker is the one for docker. Any attribute is a subcommand, with underscores turned into hyphens, and keywords become flags: Docker().ps(a=True) runs docker ps -a. Calling the object directly also works, as in Docker()('logs', 'web'). Each call returns what the command printed and raises IOError if it fails. Docker().compose(...) runs a compose subcommand, using the older standalone docker-compose if it is installed and docker compose otherwise.
Docker(no_creds=True) runs docker with a copy of your Docker config that has the credential helpers (credsStore and credHelpers) taken out, kept in ~/.fastops/config. It applies only when the DOCKR_RUNTIME environment variable is unset or set to docker.
Dockerfile.build saves the Dockerfile into the folder path and builds it with docker compose build. That command uses the daemon’s BuildKit and does not need the buildx plugin. build returns the tag. test runs a command in a throwaway container and returns True if the command exits with status 0. drun runs a container and returns its output. text:
A Dockerfile is a list of instructions, one per line, each starting with a keyword such as FROM, RUN or COPY. The private helpers below (_from, _run, _copy and so on) each format one instruction. They take care of the details that are easy to get wrong by hand: joining an image and its tag, writing a command list in the JSON form Docker expects, and chaining several shell commands into a single RUN with &&. You do not call them directly; the Dockerfile methods do.
The tests after the helpers show the exact line each one writes.

assert _instr('RUN', 'echo hello') == 'RUN echo hello'
assert _from('python', '3.11') == 'FROM python:3.11'
assert _from('ubuntu', as_='builder') == 'FROM ubuntu AS builder'

assert _run('apt-get update') == 'RUN apt-get update'
r = _run(['apt-get update', 'apt-get install -y curl'])
assert 'apt-get update && ' in r

Dockerfile holds the instruction lines in order. It has one method per Dockerfile keyword, named in lower case, and each method returns a new Dockerfile with the line added, so calls chain. print shows the file, and save writes it, to ./Dockerfile by default. text:
These functions wrap the Docker command-line tool for the usual loop: build an image from a Dockerfile, run a container from it, and check that a command succeeds inside it. They need Docker installed and its daemon running.
Cli is a small base class for wrapping a command-line tool, and Docker is the one for docker. Any attribute is a subcommand, with underscores turned into hyphens, and keywords become flags: Docker().ps(a=True) runs docker ps -a. Calling the object directly also works, as in Docker()('logs', 'web'). Each call returns what the command printed and raises IOError if it fails. Docker().compose(...) runs a compose subcommand, using the older standalone docker-compose if it is installed and docker compose otherwise.
Docker(no_creds=True) runs docker with a copy of your Docker config that has the credential helpers (credsStore and credHelpers) taken out, kept in ~/.fastops/config. It applies only when the DOCKR_RUNTIME environment variable is unset or set to docker.
Dockerfile.build saves the Dockerfile into the folder path and builds it with docker compose build. That command uses the daemon’s BuildKit and does not need the buildx plugin. build returns the tag. test runs a command in a throwaway container and returns True if the command exits with status 0. drun runs a container and returns its output. With detach=True it starts the container in the background and returns its ID. The ports dictionary maps container ports to host ports.

text:
App builders
Five methods added to Dockerfile install dependencies: inst_uv, uv_deps, uv_project, with_uv and packages. The builders further down use them.
A single-stage Dockerfile installs dependencies in the final image. A multi-stage Dockerfile installs dependencies in a builder stage and copies the result into a separate runtime stage.
inst_uv is the single-stage way to install a Python project. It installs uv with pip, copies pyproject.toml in, runs uv sync --no-dev and puts the project’s .venv on the PATH. With req=True it copies requirements.txt instead and installs it into the system Python.
Three options make the single-stage install reproducible and quick to rebuild. lock=True copies uv.lock too and syncs with --frozen. The image then has exactly the versions in the lock file. bytecode=True compiles the installed packages to bytecode in the image. The app then does not compile them each time it starts. deps_first=True splits the install in two layers: uv_deps syncs the dependencies alone, then uv_project copies the project in and syncs it. Docker reuses the dependency layer until pyproject.toml or uv.lock changes. A code change rebuilds only the second half. mid runs commands between dependency installation and project installation, such as a download the app needs at run time. compile names source folders to compile to bytecode after the project sync.
The single-stage recipe pulls only from Docker Hub and installs uv with pip. The multi-stage recipe pulls uv’s image from ghcr.io, and GitHub’s registry answers some hosting providers’ addresses with 403 Forbidden for anonymous pulls. A Hetzner server building a Compose stack hit this. Use multistage=False, lock=True on such servers.
with_uv is the multi-stage way. It adds a build stage in uv’s image that installs the dependencies pinned in uv.lock, with uv’s cache kept between builds, and then starts the runtime stage from image. The caller copies the result across, as python_app does with copy(wd, wd, from_='builder').
packages installs system packages with apt-get. Pass the names as separate arguments, not as one list. With no names it does nothing. A builder can write .packages(*listify(pkgs)) without checking whether pkgs is empty.

text:
Secrets
secret_set and secret_get are for sensitive values such as API tokens and tunnel tokens. secret_set stores the value in the system keychain through the keyring package, for example the macOS Keychain. Where there is no keychain, as on most servers and CI machines, that step fails. By default (save=False) secret_set then raises RuntimeError and writes nothing, because it never saves a secret in plain text unless you ask. Pass save=True to also call env_set, which writes the value, in plain text, to the .env file and sets it in os.environ. With save=True and no working keychain, secret_set issues a UserWarning that names the .env file holding the only copy, and still writes it.
secret_get looks in the keychain, then os.environ, then the .env file, and returns default if none of them has the key. On a server, the usual way to supply secrets is as environment variables, set at boot by cloud-init or a systemd EnvironmentFile=.
